concept.name: LiteLLM
concept.title: LiteLLM, for Customer Success
concept.definition: LiteLLM is a self-hosted AI gateway that sits between a customer's applications and many model providers. Apps send one OpenAI-style request; LiteLLM routes it, tracks spend, and controls who can use which models.
concept.problem: Without a gateway, each app talks to each vendor separately. Keys scatter, spend is hard to explain, switching models means changing application code, and an outage at one provider can stop the product.

goals: understand customer architecture discussions about LiteLLM
explain the gateway accurately to customers
recognize spend, access, and reliability implications

nodes.label: Customer's AI Apps
nodes.caption: chatbots, agents, tools
nodes.description: The products teams ship that need language models. They should call one gateway instead of every vendor API.

nodes.label: Virtual Keys
nodes.caption: access with limits
nodes.description: LiteLLM issues its own keys to teams and apps. A virtual key can allow specific models, set a budget, and be revoked without rotating the real vendor keys.

nodes.label: LiteLLM Gateway
nodes.caption: one endpoint for many models
nodes.description: A self-hosted proxy that accepts OpenAI-compatible requests and talks to the configured providers. Customers usually mean this service when they say they use LiteLLM.

nodes.label: Route and Fallback
nodes.caption: pick a working model
nodes.description: LiteLLM can send traffic across providers or regions, retry failures, and fall back to another model if one is down or rate-limited.

nodes.label: Spend and Budgets
nodes.caption: track and cap cost
nodes.description: Every request can be attributed to a key, team, or user. Budgets can stop new requests when a limit is reached, instead of discovering the bill later.

nodes.label: Guardrails
nodes.caption: policy checks
nodes.description: Optional checks such as PII masking or prompt-injection filters that can run on a model call. Not every customer enables them.

nodes.label: Model Providers
nodes.caption: OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and more
nodes.description: The actual model vendors and hosted endpoints. LiteLLM keeps their different APIs behind one interface so apps do not integrate each one separately.

nodes.label: Admin View
nodes.caption: who used what
nodes.description: The LiteLLM dashboard for keys, teams, spend, and request health. Operations and finance often use this to see AI usage.

groups.label: LiteLLM — one gateway for many models
groups.description: The self-hosted AI gateway customers place in front of model providers to unify access, routing, and spend control.

chapters.title: Where LiteLLM sits
chapters.explanation: A customer's AI apps need models from several vendors. LiteLLM sits in the middle as one gateway, so those apps do not each integrate OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and the rest separately.
takeaways: LiteLLM is the gateway in front of models

chapters.title: One request, many models
chapters.explanation: Apps send an OpenAI-compatible request to LiteLLM. The gateway translates that request to the chosen provider and returns a consistent response, so switching models is a gateway change, not an application rewrite.
takeaways: Model swaps stay in the gateway

chapters.title: Access with virtual keys
chapters.explanation: Teams do not need a copy of every vendor API key. LiteLLM issues virtual keys that can limit models, budgets, and rate limits. Revoking a virtual key cuts off an app without rotating the real provider credentials.
takeaways: A virtual key is LiteLLM access, not a vendor password
Budgets and model permissions live on the key

chapters.title: Stay up and stay in budget
chapters.explanation: If a provider fails or rate-limits, LiteLLM can retry or fall back to another model. At the same time it attributes spend to keys and teams, and can stop requests when a budget is reached. The admin view is how operators and finance see that activity.
takeaways: The admin view answers who spent what

roleRelevance.title: Why this matters for a Customer Success Manager
points: When a customer says they use LiteLLM, they usually mean a shared gateway, not a Python library inside one app.
Ask whether apps call vendors directly or go through the gateway. That changes how you diagnose outages, spend spikes, and model-switch requests.
Spend questions belong on virtual keys, teams, and the admin view, not on each application's logs.
An Anthropic or OpenAI outage may not be a product incident if fallback is already configured in the gateway.
SSO, audit logs, and contracted support are LiteLLM Enterprise add-ons. The open-source gateway already covers unified access, virtual keys, budgets, and routing.

contextCards.title: How the pieces fit
points: Apps send one OpenAI-style request to LiteLLM.
A virtual key authorizes the call and can carry a budget.
LiteLLM routes the call to a model provider and records the spend.

contextCards.title: Terms customers may use
points: Proxy, AI gateway, and LiteLLM often mean the same shared service.
The Python SDK is a library one app can import. The gateway is what the whole organization calls.
OpenAI-compatible means apps keep the OpenAI request shape even when the backend is Anthropic, Bedrock, or Azure.

contextCards.title: Why customers use it
points: Stop integrating every vendor API in every app.
See and cap AI spend before the invoice arrives.
Change models without starting a new application project.
